title: the word Francis (the pope) can't stop saying
hook: the word Francis (the pope) can't stop saying

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa of Ávila, and prayer as friendship. Your line was: talk to him like a friend. What did you say, stirring the pot? Day twenty.

In 2013, a man from Buenos Aires who used to ride the bus to work became pope and took a name no pope had ever used: Francis, after the rich kid from Assisi you met on day eight. Journalists started counting the words he used most. One kept coming up, in sermons, in interviews, off the cuff to crowds. He called a whole year after it. He titled a book after it. Asked once, early on, to describe himself, he said, in effect: a sinner the Lord has looked upon. Pope Francis led the Church until his death in 2025, and if you had to sum him up in one word, most people would pick the same one. Today, mercy.
screen: `A POPE WHO RODE THE BUS.` → `ONE WORD KEPT COMING UP.` → `A SINNER THE LORD LOOKED UPON.`

segments.voice: The Latin word is misericordia. Take it apart and it's two words: miseri, the wretched, the ones in trouble, and cor, the heart. Mercy is a heart that goes out to someone in misery. Not a verdict. A heart. The Bible's Hebrew has a word for it that comes from the word for a mother's womb, the kind of love you feel for a child you carried. Luke's Gospel puts it at the center of what Jesus asks, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Pope Francis took his motto from an old sermon by Bede, an English monk, about the day Jesus called Matthew, a tax collector everyone despised. Jesus looked at him, Bede says, with mercy, and chose him. In Latin: miserando atque eligendo. By having mercy, and by choosing. Francis said that was his own story. That's where today's line comes from. Francis kept saying that people who can't show mercy are often people who have never let themselves receive it. You can't give away what you've never been handed. So the first step is to accept it, to let God, or someone, look at you with mercy and choose you anyway, the way Jesus looked at Matthew. That's hard. Most of us are much harder on ourselves than on anyone else. Then it flows outward: forgiving, feeding, visiting, going toward people in trouble. Catholics call these the works of mercy, and remember Francis of Assisi kissing the leper's hand? That's the same heart. Confession from day twelve is the Church's way of saying it out loud: you're forgiven. Start there.
screen: `MISERICORDIA — A HEART FOR THE WRETCHED.` · `BE YE THEREFORE MERCIFUL.` · `BY HAVING MERCY, AND BY CHOOSING.` · `YOU CAN'T GIVE WHAT YOU WERE NEVER HANDED.` · then, large: `START WITH YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of one thing you're still angry at yourself about. Something small or something big. Picture someone who loves you looking at it, and at you, without flinching. Not excusing it. Just looking at you with a heart that goes out to you. Breathe slowly, and let yourself be looked at like that. If you pray, you can let that look be God's. The bell holds the time.
Mercy. Misericordia: a heart that goes out to someone in trouble, received first, then given away. Twentieth word.
Your line: start with yourself. Today, the next time you make a mistake, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a friend who made it. Day twenty.

howItsDone: Catholics practice the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and forgiving injuries, and celebrate Divine Mercy Sunday on the Sunday after Easter.

original.note: Latin: mercy. from miseri, the wretched, and cor, the heart.
